list.listitem: Consider the diagnosis of chronic obstructive pulmonary (lung) disease (COPD) in patients with chronic and progressive dyspnea, cough, and sputum production, a history of recurrent lower respiratory tract infections, and/or a history of exposure to risk factors for the disease, and obtain spirometry.

Active case-finding among high-risk patients should be considered.C GOLD 2024 (Global Initiative for Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease) suggests screening for COPD at lung cancer screening programs or when incidental lung abnormalities are found on imaging that may indicate the presence of COPD.C
Consider arterial blood gas (ABG) measurement for patients with forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1) less than 50% or clinical signs of respiratory failure or right-sided heart failure.C
Smoking cessation is the cornerstone of therapy.A

Vaccinations recommended for those with COPD include influenza and respiratory syncytial virus (the latter, for those over age 60 years) A and COVID-19 and pneumococcus B. Tdap vaccination is recommended for people with COPD not vaccinated in adolescence and Zoster vaccination for those with COPD who are over age 50 years.B

First-line therapy for COPD management is single (GOLD group A) or dual long-acting inhaled bronchodilator therapy with a long-acting beta2-agonist and long-acting muscarinic antagonist (LABA/LAMA) for GOLD groups B and E.A For patients in Group E, addition of inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) should be considered in patients with blood eosinophil counts >300 cells/mL.B Education in proper inhaler technique is important.
Exercise training programs, including Qigong, and pulmonary rehabilitation programs improve exercise tolerance and reduce symptoms of dyspnea and fatigue.A
Comprehensive self-management training may reduce COPD-related hospitalizations but data are conflicting.C

Oxygen has been shown to improve survival in patients with COPD and severe hypoxemia (but not moderate).A The American Thoracic Society recommends long-term home oxygen for at least 15 hours daily for patients with COPD and severe hypoxia (see definitions in Treatment).B

background.definition: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a chronic lung disorder characterized by progressive airflow limitation that is not fully reversible. COPD is usually caused by smoking. The airflow limitation is usually progressive and associated with an abnormal inflammatory response of the lung to noxious particles or gases. In 2023, GOLD changed their definition of COPD to “a heterogeneous lung condition characterized by chronic respiratory symptoms (dyspnea, cough, sputum production and/or exacerbations) due to abnormalities of the airways (bronchitis, bronchiolitis) and/or alveoli (emphysema) that cause persistent, often progressive, airflow obstruction." COPD is preventable and treatable. Some patients have significant extrapulmonary effects that contribute to disease severity.

list.listitem: A study of COPD using birth cohorts from 1919 to 1950 conducted in Northern Sweden found that the 10-year cumulative incidence of COPD in 1109 patients reporting respiratory symptoms at baseline (representing 76.6% of the original symptomatic cohort and 16.7% of the total cohort) was 13.5% using GOLD criteria.

In a national prevalence survey of English adults older than 35 years, 13.3% (95% CI 12.6-14.0) had spirometry-defined COPD. Over 80% reported no respiratory diagnosis. Even among those with severe COPD, only 46.8% reported a respiratory diagnosis.

The pooled international prevalence of COPD was 7.6% from 37 studies in 28 different countries; the pooled spirometric estimate was 8.9%. In a more recent systematic review and meta-analysis of global prevalence of COPD, the prevalence was 9.23% (95% credible interval [CrI] 8.16%-10.36%) in men and 6.16% (95% CrI 5.41%-6.95%) in women.

The Burden of Obstructive Lung Diseases study, conducted in 29 countries, reported worse lung function in 2020 than earlier studies, with an overall prevalence of COPD of 11.8% for men and 8.5% for women; prevalence of COPD was 3% to 11% even among never-smokers. Prevalence of chronic airflow obstruction, defined as post-bronchodilator one-second forced expiratory volume to forced vital capacity ratio below the lower limit of normal was 11.2% for men and 8.6% for women Risk factors were smoking, poor education levels, working in a dusty job for ≥10 years, low body mass index (BMI), and a history of tuberculosis.

Estimated prevalence of diagnosed COPD in adults over age 18 years in the United States (2014) is about 15.7 million cases, or 6.4% of the population. Prevalence rates vary by state from <4% in Hawaii, Colorado, and Utah to >9% in Alabama, Tennessee, Kentucky, and West Virginia.

In a Swedish epidemiologic study, the prevalence of COPD based on British Thoracic Society, European Respiratory Society, GOLD, and American Thoracic Society (ATS) clinical and ATS spirometric standards was 7.6%, 14.0%, 14.1%, 12.2%, and 34.2%, respectively.
Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency affects 1 in 2000 to 5000 individuals.

Using data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Surveys 2007 to 2012, the age-standardized prevalence of asthma-COPD overlap was 1.05% (95% CI 0.7%-1.4%). A similar prevalence rate of self-reported asthma-COPD overlap of 1.9% was reported in a large population-based Norwegian study; prevalence ranged from 0.7% for those under age 40 years to 3.2% in those 60 years and over. These data stand in contrast to reports listed in the section on Other Impact where up to 30% of patients with COPD report a history of asthma.

Beginning in 2020, GOLD no longer referred to asthma-COPD overlap, and emphasized that these conditions have differences in the involved inflammatory cells and mediators although some patients with COPD have an inflammatory pattern with increased eosinophils and ILC2 cells, similar to asthma. Asthma may be a risk factor for COPD; however, airway hyper-responsiveness can exist without a clinical diagnosis of asthma and is an independent predictor of COPD.

In a systematic review of economic costs of COPD in the United States, the annual cost (direct and indirect) was $38.8 billion in 2005; more than half was direct. Per patient costs ranged from $2700 to $5900 annually.
Authors of a review paper noted a projected cost of COPD in the United States of approximately $50 billion in 2010, including $30 billion in direct healthcare expenditures.
In 2000, patients with COPD had 8 million physician outpatient visits, 1.5 million emergency room visits, and 726,000 hospitalizations.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) listed chronic lower respiratory disease as the fourth leading cause of death in 2019, with 156,979 attributed deaths. In 2021, COVID-19 replaced COPD as the third leading cause of death. In 2022, COPD was ranked 6th with 147,382 attributed deaths.
In a report on U.S. burden of disease, COPD was among the five conditions responsible for the largest number of years of life lost due to premature mortality.

In the Global Burden of Disease study 2017, approimately 545 million people worldwide had a chronic respiratory disease, an increase of 39.8% compared with 1990. COPD was ranked as the 3rd leading cause of death worldwide (7% of all deaths). COPD accounted for the majority of chronic respiratory disease-associated disability-adjusted life years lost.

In the Genetic Epidemiology of COPD study - an observational, multicenter, longitudinal analysis of over 10,000 subjects with a 10+ pack-year cigarette smoking history with and without COPD - comorbidities associated with COPD were coronary artery disease, gastroesophageal reflux, heart failure, hypertension, obstructive sleep apnea, osteoporosis, peripheral vascular disease, and stroke.
In a study in a managed care population, patients with COPD had higher comorbidity than age-matched controls across all age groups.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 11 studies found higher rates of the following comorbidities than for non-COPD controls: cardiovascular disease [OR 1.90, 95% CI 1.59-2.28), cerebrovascular disease (OR 1.84, 95% CI 1.47-2.31), hypertension (OR 1.45, 95% CI 1.31-1.61), diabetes mellitus (OR 1.22, 95% CI 1.07-1.38), neurological and psychiatric disorders (OR 1.78, 95% CI 1.48-2.14), gut and renal disorders (OR 1.96, 95% CI 1.43-2.68), musculoskeletal disorders (OR 1.51, 95% CI 1.27-1.78), non-COPD respiratory comorbidities (OR 2.81, 95% CI 2.52-3.14), and cancer (OR 1.67, 95% CI 1.25-2.23).

Mortality following myocardial infarction (MI) was higher for patients with COPD, both in-hospital (4.6% vs. 3.2%) and at 180 days (12.8% vs. 7.7%) based on a UK database study. Potential explanations for this gap included delayed diagnosis, timing and use of reperfusion of a ST-elevation MI, use of angiography after a non-ST elevation MI and use of secondary prevention medicines.
Coronary artery calcification appears to be more prevalent in patients with COPD and is associated with increased mortality.

Among patients with COPD, age over 60 years, BMI <25 kg/m2, 60+ pack-years, and the presence of emphysema were independently associated with lung cancer diagnosis. Patients with high scores (scores 7-10) on the lung cancer screening score had a 3.5-fold increased risk of lung cancer vs. low scoring patients (score <7).
Among patients with lung cancer, the presence of COPD is associated with poorer survival with a hazard ratio (HR) of 1.18, 95% CI 1.11-1.25 for 5-year overall survival.

Asthma is present in about 20% of people with COPD and results in increased morbidity and possibly mortality. In a Canadian database study of 9053 patients with COPD, 2717 (30%) had a history of asthma which was associated with COPD and respiratory-related hospitalizations but not all-cause mortality.

The pooled global prevalence of osteoporosis in patients with COPD from 58 studies was 38% (95% CI 34%-43%). Other significant risk factors for osteoporosis in patients with COPD were BMI <18.5 kg/m2 (OR 4.26) and the presence of sarcopenia (OR 3.65).

Patients with COPD also appear to have impaired cognitive function compared to healthy controls, although they are not as impaired as patients with Alzheimer's disease. In one follow-up study, about one quarter of 1425 patients with COPD and normal baseline cognitive function developed mild cognitive impairment at a mean of 5 years. Longer duration of COPD was associated with the greatest risk of impairment.
Patients with COPD demonstrate accelerated progression of frailty compared with patients with normal spirometry, with an additional annual increase of 0.2 (95% CI 0.1-0.2).

Environmental and genetic factors. GOLD 2024 notes that COPD is the end result of a complex dynamic of environmental and gene interactions. Environmental factors include smoking (cigarette and other types of tobacco) and exposures to biomass, organic and inorganic dusts, chemical agents, fumes and air pollutants. The most relevant genetic risk factor for COPD are mutations in the SERPINA1 gene that lead to α1-antitrypsin deficiency although many other genetic variants leading to reduced lung function and risk of COPD have been identified.

The ongoing Genetic Epidemiology of COPD study was designed to identify COPD genotypes and phenotypes along with factors influencing phenotypic expression of COPD such as sex, race and age. Thus far over 80 genomic regions associated with COPD have been identified. Women with COPD were found to report more dyspnea and have a higher risk of COPD exacerbations while African Americans have worse health status and are more likely to also have asthma.
Cigarette smoking, as well as passive exposure to cigarette smoke, is the largest contributor; occupational exposure accounts for 10% to 20% of cases.
Other contributors are occupational dust, chemicals, and indoor air pollution.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 18 studies found that an increase of 10-μg/m³ in particulate matter with aerodynamic diameters of ≤2.5 μm, as found with air pollution, was associated with a 2.5% (95% CI 1.8%-3.2%) increase in COPD hospitalizations (OR 1.025; 95% CI 1.018-1.032), and a 1.5% (95% CI 0.9%-2.2%) increase in COPD mortality (OR 1.015; 95% CI 1.009-1.022). In a study of deceased veterans with prior COPD, there was a 1.05 fold (95% CI 1.02-1.09) mortality risk increase for each 10 μg/m3 increase in daily wintertime PM2.5, with older and Black individuals displaying elevated risk.

In one study, airflow obstruction was consistently associated with poverty at individual and community levels, with an absolute increase in FEV1/FVC of 0.36% (95% CI 0.22-0.49) per unit increase in wealth score. In another study, individuals in the lowest socioeconomic strata were at least twice as likely to have poor outcomes as those in the highest stratum.

Reduced lung growth during gestation; childhood lung disease; and early, severe childhood respiratory infections are also associated with COPD. In fact, one study estimated that about half of patients with COPD develop the disease due to abnormal lung growth and development, with declining function over time.

The pathologic changes include chronic inflammation, changes in mucin production, and structural changes in the lung from repeated injury and repair. These changes cause airflow limitation, gas trapping, and abnormalities in gas exchange. These changes cause airflow limitation, gas trapping, and abnormalities in gas exchange.

The inflammation is likely an amplification of the normal inflammatory response to chronic irritants (most often cigarette smoke). The response includes increased numbers of macrophages, activated neutrophils and lymphocytes that recruit inflammatory cells into the terminal air spaces which release proteinases that damage the extracellular lung matrix and cause ineffective repair of elastin and other matrix components. Inflammation also results in narrowing and obstruction of the peripheral airways causing airway collapse.

Normal airway mucus, which is produced by surface goblet and secretory cells, is altered in individuals with COPD. Submucosal gland hyperplasia along with presence of cytokines increase mucous production that can occlude airways.

Structural changes include parenchymal destruction and fibrosis; the former resulting in decreased air exchange. Abnormalities in microvascular blood flow worsen as COPD progresses. Structural changes also can include intimal hyperplasia and smooth muscle hypertrophy caused by hypoxic vasoconstriction of small pulmonary arteries; these changes can result in pulmonary hypertension.

Authors of one study found that decreased mucosal surface secretory IgA levels in patients with COPD was associated with invasion of bacteria across the epithelial barrier potentially driving persistent inflammation and airway wall remodeling.

Excessive prostaglandin production can increase susceptibility to infection associated with COPD exacerbations and promote inadequate alveolar repair. Inhibition of endogenous prostanoid synthesis or signaling may have therapeutic potential.
The gut microbiome may contribute to COPD pathogenesis.

Patients with the Z allele associated with marked reductions in alpha-1 antitrypsin (1%-2% of cases) have reduced levels of this protease inhibitor and are more susceptible to developing COPD, especially from cigarette smoking. Increased alveolar damage is caused by neutrophil elastase, resulting in loss of elastic recoil and airflow obstruction.

list.listitem: The USPSTF (2022) recommends against screening for COPD with spirometry ("D" recommendation), B whereas the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI) recommends spirometry for all smokers 45 years or older.C Active case finding should be considered in high risk persons.C
GOLD 2024 suggests screening for COPD at lung cancer screening programs or when incidental lung abnormalities are found on imaging that may indicate the presence of COPD.C
Smoking cessation is a key element in the prevention of COPD; counseling delivered by healthcare providers and legislated smoking bans improve quit rates.A

Vaccinations recommended by the CDC and GOLD 2024 for those with COPD include influenza and respiratory syncytial virus (the latter, for those over age 60 years) A and COVID-19 and pneumococcus B. Tdap vaccination is recommended for people with COPD not vaccinated in adolescence and Zoster vaccination for those with COPD who are over age 50 years.B

Secondary prevention strategies to improve symptoms and quality of life and/or reduce exacerbations include individualized pharmacologic treatment, pulmonary rehabilitation and noninvasive mechanical ventilation.A (GOLD 2020 guidelines)

Oxygen therapy in patients with severe resting chronic hypoxemia improves survival.A (GOLD 2020 guidelines) Home noninvasive mechanical ventilation using bilevel positive airway pressure may lower mortality risk in patients with severe chronic hypercapnia and a history of hospitalization for respiratory failure.B

The USPSTF (2022) recommends against screening of COPD with spirometry. In the systematic evidence review for this update, the reviewers found insufficient evidence to quantify the benefits and harms of COPD screening with questionnaires or handheld spirometry, and there was little available evidence to estimate treatment benefits in screen-detected populations for smoking cessation or reduced mortality.

The USPSTF (2021) recommends annual screening for lung cancer with low-dose computed tomography in patients age 50 to 80 years with a 20-pack-year smoking history who still smoke or quit within the past 15 years.B Screening should be discontinued once a person has not smoked for 15 years or develops a health problem that substantially limits life expectancy or willingness to have curative lung surgery.

GOLD 2024 recommend consideration of active case finding in patients with COPD symptoms or risk factors (eg, recurrent chest infections in early life, >20 pack-years of smoking) given that FEV1 and FVC predict all-cause mortality independent of tobacco smoking; however, there are no data indicating that screening spirometry is helpful for improving COPD outcomes or directing management in patients identified before significant symptom development.

To identify risk factors predictive of COPD, investigators followed 801 participants who did not have COPD at age 45 years for 8 years. Those with a pre-bronchodilator pre- FEV1/FVC z-score less than -1.26 (lowest 10th percentile) had a 36-fold increased risk of developing COPD (risk ratio 35.8, 95% CI 8.9 to 144). Interestingly respiratory symptoms, post-bronchodilator spirometry, diffusing capacity, and static lung volumes did not improve on the classification.

GOLD 2024 suggests leveraging lung imaging for COPD screening based on lung cancer and COPD sharing common risk factors and studies showing that screening for COPD at lung cancer screening identifies airway obstruction in up to half and emphysema in 68-73% of individuals with no prior diagnosis of COPD.

If considering conducting case finding, use of a novel risk score based on electronic record data of age, smoking status, dyspnea, prescriptions of salbutamol and prescriptions of antibiotics discriminated between patients with and without undiagnosed COPD (c-statistic 0.74, 95% CI 0.68-0.80).

In a Canadian multiyear study, a massive effort to identify persons with undiagnosed asthma or COPD ultimately identified 508 of almost 50,000 who were screened (~1%). They were randomized to intensive specialist led care strictly adhering to guidelines, or usual care largely from primary care doctors. The benefits for those in the intervention group were small and not clinically important, with no reduction in emergency department visits or hospitalizations. This study will be touted by pulmonologists as a success, when it is actually a failed intervention.

In a clustered RCT in the Netherlands, community subjects ≥65 years of age with dyspnea or reduced exercise tolerance were randomly allocated to usual care or a case-finding strategy for heart failure or COPD. The case-finding strategy consisted of history-taking, physical examination, blood tests, electrocardiography, spirometry, and echocardiography. A new diagnosis of HF or COPD was made in more individuals in the case-finding group vs. usual care group with a cumulative incidence of 34% vs 2% for heart failure and 17% vs. 2% for COPD. However, we don't know if these additional diagnoses improved outcomes such as mortality or hospitalizaiton.

Investigators in a study of 105,630 randomly-chosen adults from a Danish contemporary population-based cohort identified 8,064 individuals under age 50 years with 10 pack-years or greater of tobacco consumption. Of these individuals, 15% had early COPD, of whom 58% were current smokers. During the 14.4-year follow-up of these individuals, there were 117 acute COPD-related hospitalizations, 227 acute hospitalizations with pneumonia, and 185 deaths. Those with early COPD had multivariable adjusted HR of 6.42 (95% CI 3.39-12.2) for acute COPD hospitalization, 2.03 (95% CI 1.43-2.88) for acute pneumonia hospitalization, and 1.79 (95% CI 1.28-2.52) for all-cause mortality.

Screen for alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency in symptomatic adults with persistent obstruction on pulmonary function testing (PFT) or asymptomatic adults with persistent obstruction on PFT who have a minimal history of smoking, a family history of COPD, or a significant history of occupational exposure.

Canadian Thoracic Society guidelines (2025) conditionally recommend testing all patients for A1AT deficiency at the time of diagnosis, as well as those with adult-onset asthma and persistent airay obstruction, and patients with unexplained bronchiectasis. They recommend genetic testing for the SERPINA1 gene as the initial test if clinical suspicion is high, and serum A1AT levels if suspicion is moderate followed by genetic testing if the A1AT level is less than 23 umol/l (1.2 g/L).

Although smoking is not the only risk factor, smoking cessation is a key element in the prevention of COPD. GOLD 2024 now includes additional information on pharmacotherapies for smoking cessation. In one RCT of smoking cessation in patients with asymptomatic airway obstruction, all-cause mortality was lower in the group receiving the smoking intervention. There is no evidence supporting effectiveness and safety of e-cigarettes as an aid for smoking cessation.

A diet rich in beta-carotene and vitamin E was associated with a lower risk of developing COPD in 1 large RCT.However, in an RCT of beta-carotene and vitamin E supplements for smokers, there was no benefit and possible harm.
Management of acute exacerbations of COPD is addressed in a separate chapter.
In a small study, a diet rich in omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids reduced dyspnea (1 point on a 10-point scale) and improved walking distance (5%) in patients with COPD.

Dietary nitrate supplementation in the form of 140 mL of nitrate-rich beetroot juice (12.9 mmol nitrate) was more effective than placebo in improving exercise capacity as measured by the incremental shuttle walk test distance (estimated treatment effect of 30 m; 95% CI 10-40 m).

In an RCT with 81 patients with muscle wasting and COPD, randomization to 3 portions of nutritional supplementation daily (enriched with leucine, vitamin D and polyunsaturated fatty acids) vs. placebo prior to pulmonary rehabilitation resulted in greater activity participation, reduced anxiety and depression scores and stable (vs. decreased) quality of life at one year.
Influenza vaccination can reduce serious illness in patients with COPD and likely reduces COPD exacerbations.

Pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine (PPV) is also recommended for adults over age 18 years with COPD, if they have never received a pneumococcal vaccine previously (or status is unknown). The recommendation is for PCV15 (a pneumococcal conjugated vaccine) followed by PPSV23 (a pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine) OR one dose PCV20 (a pneumococcal conjugated vaccine). Authors of a Cochrane review of 12 trials with 2171 participants concluded that PPSV reduces episodes of community acquired pneumonia (number needed to treat [NNT] = 21), but not mortality or hospital admissions. It also decreased the likelihood of an acute exacerbation of COPD (NNT = 8, 95% CI 5-58).
The CDC recommends dTAP vaccination in patients with COPD who were not vaccinated as adolescents to protect against pertussis, and Zoster vaccine to protect against shingles.
Reduce exposure to occupational dust and chemicals and indoor air pollution.

A well-designed study randomized 116 former smokers with moderate to severe COPD to the use of an active HEPA filter air cleaner or a sham air cleaner for 6 months. The active air cleaner was effective in decreasing the rates of moderate exacerbations (0.4 vs 1.25 over 6 months) and rescue medication use.
Drugs for reducing exacerbations (see chapter on COPD, acute exacerbation)

Drugs recommended for reducing COPD exacerbations depend on COPD group (mild to very severe) and frequency of exacerbations and include inhaled bronchodilators, inhaled corticosteroids, a daily macrolide, N-acetyl cysteine, roflumilast, and theophylline (see below under Drug Therapy and also in the chapter noted above).
There is weak evidence, largely based on observational studies, that statin use is associated with a decreased risk of COPD exacerbation.

GOLD 2024 concluded that attending a PR program lasting 6-8 weeks improves dyspnea, health status and exercise tolerance; reduces symptoms of anxiety and depression; and reduces hospitalizations for those with a recent (4 or fewer weeks) exacerbation.

The American Thoracic Society (2023) also recommends pulmonary rehabilitation for adults with stable COPD (moderate-quality evidence) and after hospitalization for COPD exacerbation (moderate-quality evidence). They also make a strong recommendation for offering a choice of center-based or telerehabilitation for patients with chronic respiratory disease (moderate-quality evidence) and a conditional recommendation for offering either supervised maintenance or usual care after initial pulmonary rehabilitation for adults with COPD (low-quality evidence).

Authors of a meta-analysis of 10 RCTs found a reduction in overall rate of hospitalizations following PR vs. placebo (0.97 vs. 0.62 hospitalizations/patient-year) and a significantly lower 12-month admission rate in 5 before and after PR studies (1.24 vs. 0.47 hospitalizations/patient-year).

Using a Medicare database, investigators identified 197,376 patients older than 65 years who were hospitalized for COPD of whom only 1.5% had received PR within 90 days of discharge. Using propensity score matching to those not receiving PR, initiating PR within 90 days was associated with fewer deaths at 1 year (7.3% vs. 14.1%; HR 0.50; 95% CI 0.42-0.59; NNT = 15).

GOLD 2024 concluded that in patients with severe resting chronic hypoxemia, long-term oxygen therapy improves survival. In patients with stable COPD and resting or exercise-induced moderate desaturation, however, long-term oxygen treatment should not be prescribed routinely but on a case-by-case basis.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 21 RCTs and 12 observational studies including 51,085 patients in home settings, found home NIV using bilevel positive airway pressure compared with no device was significantly associated with lower mortality risk (22.3% vs. 28.6%, respectively; NNT = 15), but no significant difference in quality of life. A home mechanical ventilator compared with no device was significantly associated with fewer hospital admissions in one study, but no significant differences in mortality or quality of life. Overall risk of bias was judged to be moderate to high.
COPD exacerbation action plans reduce the likelihood of hospitalization and increase the use of corticosteroids and antibiotics; the effect on mortality is unknown.
Surgical therapies, described below, can reduce symptoms and improve quality of life in selected patients.
Palliative approaches can relieve symptoms in patients with advanced COPD.
The characteristic symptoms of COPD are chronic and progressive dyspnea, cough, and sputum production.C

The American College of Physicians (ACP), American College of Chest Physicians, ATS, GOLD and the European Respiratory Society recommend spirometry to confirm the diagnosis.C A post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC ratio <0.70 confirms the presence of persistent airflow limitation.
Consider measurement of ABG tensions in patients with peripheral oxygen saturation <92% or clinical signs of respiratory failure (PCO2 >45) or right-sided heart failure.C

list.listitem: Suspect COPD in patients with chronic respiratory symptoms, a history of recurrent lower respiratory tract infections, and/or a history of exposure to risk factors for the disease. Risk factors include host factors such as congenital abnormalities or childhood lung infection, tobacco use, and occupational or environmental (eg, cooking and heating fuel) exposures. Also ask about a family history of COPD or other chronic respiratory disease.

The characteristic symptoms are chronic and progressive dyspnea, cough, and sputum production. Other signs and symptoms include hyperinflation of the chest with increased anterior–posterior diameter; use of accessory muscles of respiration; purse-lip breathing; and symptoms of right-sided heart failure including lower extremity edema.

In one study of newly diagnosed patients, 85% presented with cough, 70% with exertional dyspnea, and 45% with increased sputum production; the mean duration of symptoms was 12 months. Most were in GOLD stage 0 to I (42%) or II (46%) with 12% diagnosed as stage III.

GOLD 2024 also notes the presence of a pattern of symptom development with most patients becoming aware of increased breathlessness, more frequent or prolonged “winter colds,” and some social restriction for a number of years before seeking medical help.

In a 10-year cumulative incidence study, symptoms predictive of COPD differed in women versus men with cough, sputum production, and chronic-productive cough predictive in women and dyspnea and wheeze predictive in men.
Assess smoking history; a history of over 40 pack-years of cigarette smoking is strongly associated with COPD.
A genetic mutation should be suspected in patients with emphysema who are younger than 50 years, have a positive family history, primarily basilar disease, and minimal smoking history.

Also important for treatment planning are a history of exacerbations or hospitalizations for respiratory disorders, the presence of co-morbidities (noted above), functional status and influence of the disease on the patient’s life, and social support.

Exam findings include wheezing, evidence of lung hyperinflation (eg, hyper resonance, diminished breath sounds), signs of increased work of breathing (eg, use of accessory muscles of respiration, purse-lip breathing, increased forced expiratory time), and signs of right-sided heart failure (as above).
In patients with asthma or COPD who are dyspneic, jugular venous distension and clinical judgment are useful to rule in CHF, while absence of rales and hepatic congestion best rule it out.

As the disease progresses, patients can develop reduced exercise capacity, fatigue, and dyspnea on exertion and/or at rest. Respiratory failure can lead to right-sided heart failure (cor pulmonale); signs of right-sided heart failure are elevated jugular venous pressure, hepatomegaly, and peripheral edema.

Clinical impression is also a predictor of COPD presence. However, in a primary care study, seasoned physicians were only able to accurately identify COPD severity in about one third of patients, underestimating severity in 41% of patients and overestimating severity in 29% of patients compared with in-office spirometry results. Patient self-assessment was similarly inaccurate.

Dyspnea can be quantified and monitored using the Medical Research Council (MRC) dyspnea scale that ranges from grade 1 (not troubled by dyspnea) to grade 5 (too breathless to leave the house or breathless when dressing or undressing). Because COPD impacts patients beyond dyspnea, GOLD 2024 recommends a more comprehensive symptom questionnaire such as the Clinical COPD Questionnaire or the COPD Assessment Test (CAT) for use in clinic. CAT is an eight-item questionnaire and is available online; it assesses and quantifies the impact of COPD symptoms on health status. In one study with 161 patients, higher baseline CAT scores were seen among those with frequent COPD exacerbations; increases in CAT score were significantly associated with falls in FEV1.

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis found that CAT was a useful adjunct to clinical assessment for predicting COPD exacerbation, health status deterioration, depression, and mortality. However, the evidence did not support the recommended cutoff points of ≥10 for CAT and ≥2 for MRC as equivalents for the purpose of assessing patient symptoms.CAT was also found useful for distinguishing between those experiencing exacerbations vs. not having exacerbations in a study of patients with newly diagnosed COPD and mild airflow obstruction.

The 4-meter gait speed, 5-repetition sit-to-stand, and 6-minute step test are all well-established psychometrically and correlate with mortality, physical activity in daily life, exercise capacity, dyspnea, and quality of life.

The ACP and GOLD guidelines recommend spirometry to confirm the diagnosis in patients suspected of having COPD. FEV1/FVC of <0.70, post bronchodilator, confirms presence of persistent airflow limitation. Most guidelines do not recommend repeat spirometry for monitoring or to determine ongoing therapy. To see spirometry graphs, see GOLD 2024.

GOLD suggests that spirometry can be used to determine disease severity: mild or GOLD 1 – FEV1 ≥80% predicted; moderate or GOLD 2 - FEV1 less than 80% but ≥50% predicted; severe or GOLD 3 - FEV1 less than 50% but ≥30%; and very severe or GOLD 4 - FEV1 <30% predicted. In addition, spirometry may be helpful for therapeutic decisions in selected circumstances (e.g., discrepancy between symptoms and spirometry results, instituting interventional procedures) or for identifying rapid decline.
Consider measurement of ABG in patients with FEV1 less than 50% or clinical signs of respiratory failure or right-sided heart failure.

In patients with severe COPD, C-reactive protein (CRP) was not associated with mortality. However, a RCT found that access to point of care CRP testing helped reduce antibiotic overprescribing for patients with an acute exacerbation of COPD.

Measurement of blood eosinophils can be considered to guide use of corticosteroids, especially in patients at higher risk of COPD exacerbations.(GOLD 2024 guidelines) Blood eosinophil counts of 300 cells/μL or higher can be used to identify patients with COPD at higher risk of exacerbations who are more likely to benefit from preventive treatment with inhaled corticosteroids.

Screen for alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency in symptomatic adults with persistent obstruction on PFT or asymptomatic adults with persistent obstruction on PFT who also have a minimal history of smoking, a family history of COPD, or a significant history of occupational exposure.

Consider a CXR in patients diagnosed with stage II or higher COPD; although seldom diagnostic, it can be useful in excluding other diagnoses and establishing the presence of comorbidities (eg, heart failure).

The Institute for Clinical Systems Improvement (ICSI, 2016) and the National Collaborating Center for Chronic Conditions suggest performing a CXR for all patients; the latter group also recommends a full blood count (for anemia or polycythemia) and calculating the body mass index (BMI).

In an emergency department (ED) setting, sonographic measurement of the inferior vena cava diameter was used to distinguish cardiac from pulmonary dyspnea; values >9 mm predicted dyspnea of cardiac origin with a sensitivity of 84.4% and a specificity of 92.9% (LR+: 11.8, LR−: 0.16). In another ED study, cardiopulmonary ultrasound demonstrated an accuracy of 90% in distinguishing the cause of acute dyspnea.
Authors of a meta-analysis including four studies of ultrasound use for diagnosing COPD/asthma exacerbation reported an area under the summary receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.906.

Consider a CT scan to investigate symptoms that seem disproportionate to the spirometric impairment, to assess abnormalities identified on CXR, or to assess suitability for surgery. GOLD 2024 also suggest consideration of chest CT for patients with persistent exacerbations, FEV1 less than 45% predicted with significant hyperinflation and gas trapping, or for those who meet criteria for lung cancer screening.

In one study of 60 patients with severe COPD awaiting lung transplantation, a pulmonary artery/ascending aorta ratio >1 on CT scan outperformed echocardiography for diagnosing pulmonary hypertension in patients with severe COPD.
An ECG finding of low voltage in lead І (QRS less than 0.54 mV) is predictive of COPD (area under the curve 0.78 (95% CI 0.69-0.86).
Consider an echocardiogram if features of cor pulmonale are present (eg, jugular venous distention, peripheral edema, hepatomegaly).

Authors of one review argue for more frequent use of echocardiography in patients with COPD to identify previously unrecognized heart abnormalities such as functional tricuspid regurgitation and pulmonary resistance which may allow for initiation of appropriate treatment to improve the patient's symptoms, quality of life, and survival.

Plasma N-terminal pro-brain natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) levels appear to increase with COPD stage (II vs. III and IV), correlate with pulmonary arterial pressure, and inversely correlate with FEV1 percentage and arterial blood gas parameters; this measure can be useful for monitoring COPD progression and identifying cases of secondary pulmonary hypertension.

Authors of a meta-analysis found elevated levels of NT-proBNP in patients with COPD vs. no COPD (standard mean difference [SMD] 0.5, 95% CI 0.2-0.7; 9 studies), patients with COPD and FEV1 <50% vs. COPD and FEV1 >=50% (SMD 0.2, 95% CI 0.05-0.3; 6 studies), patients with an acute exacerbation of COPD vs. stable COPD (SMD 1.2, 95%CI 0.07- 2.3; 3 studies), and for COPD with CHF vs. without CHF (SMD 1.49 95% CI 1-2).

Exercise testing, assessed by a reduction in self-paced walking distance (e.g., self-paced 6-minute walk test) or during incremental exercise testing in a laboratory, is an indicator of health status impairment and predictor of prognosis. Walking tests can be useful for assessing disability and risk of mortality, and laboratory exercise testing using cycle or treadmill ergometry can assist in identifying cardiac diagnoses.
Please see decision support tools for ABG interpretation, interpretation of A-a gradient, and peak flow.
The BODE index can be used to determine the prognosis of patients with COPD, as can the DECAF score (Dyspena, Eosinopenia, Consolidation, Acidemia, and atrial Fibrillation).

Using two primary care UK cohorts, investigators developed a risk model using routinely gathered data to predict 12-month mortality called BARC that included 18 variables based on body mass index and blood results (B), age (A), respiratory variables (airflow obstruction, exacerbations, smoking) (R) and comorbidities (C). The score compared favorably with other risk scores including BODEx, with an area under the curve of 0.78; 95% CI 0.76-0.79 from the training set and 0.70, 95% CI 0.67-0.72 from the external set. There was acceptable accuracy in predicting probability of death in 1 year (n high-risk group, training set: expected 0.31, observed 0.30 and external dataset: expected 0.22, observed 0.27).

A decision rule (BAP-65) can be used to predict mortality, cost, and length of stay of an episode of acute exacerbation of COPD. The rule is based on age and 3 risk factors (blood urea nitrogen >25 mg/dL, altered mental status, and pulse >109 beats/minute). Risk classes are as follows: I = age 65 years or younger and no risk factors; II = age older than 65 years and no risk factors; III = 1 risk factor; IV = 2 risk factors; and V = 3 risk factors. Hospital mortality was 0.5%, 1.4%, 3.7%, 12.7%, and 26.2% for risk classes I to V, respectively, costs increased ($4300 in group I increasing to $11,473 in group V) and median length of stay increased by class (3 days in group I increasing to 7 days in group V).

A nonvalidated clinical rule predicts the likelihood of COPD based on the presence or absence of 3 factors: peak flow less than 350 L/min, definitely or possibly diminished breath sounds, and 30 pack years or more of smoking. With no factors, the likelihood of COPD is 0%; with 1 factor, it is 24%; with 2 factors, it is 39%; and with all 3, it is 49%.

Combining maximum laryngeal height of ≤4 cm (measured from the suprasternal notch to the top of the thyroid cartilage at the end of expiration) and a score of ≤18 from the Lung Function Questionnaire yielded a LR+ of 29 and a LR− of 0.26 for a diagnosis of COPD.

Suspect COPD in patients with chronic and progressive dyspnea, cough, and sputum production or a history of tobacco use, asthma, environmental exposure to dust and chemicals, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, or chronic respiratory infections.

GOLD 2024 notes that the goals of COPD assessent are to determine the severity of airflow limitation, its impact on the patients health status, and risk of future events which includes previous exacerbations and presence of comorbidities that can independently increase hospitalizations and mortality.

Order spirometry to confirm the diagnosis and establish severity based on spirometry results, the patient’s health status, and frequency of exacerbations (0 or 1 not leading to hospitalization, >1 leading to hospital admission, or >2).

The best predictor of frequent exacerbations is a previous exacerbation. GOLD category predicts exacerbations and deteriorating airflow, and is also associated with exacerbations, hospitalization and risk of death.
Actively seek presence of comorbidities (eg, diabetes, heart disease, osteoporosis, depression) and treat as appropriate.
See for a suggested approach to management of COPD.

Continuity of care matters. In an observational study using a Norwegian population registry, for patients with COPD, mortality was 2.6 times higher (95% CI 2.2-3.0) for patients in the lowest tertile of continuity compared to those with a Usual Provider of Care Index of 1.
All patients with COPD should be counseled to quit smoking, engage in physical activity, and receive appropriate vaccinations (GOLD).

In 2023, GOLD changed its classification system to assist in treatment decisions from 4 categories (A-D) to three (A,B and E) to emphasize the clinical relevance of COPD exacerbations. Groups A and B are classified as having 0-1 moderate exacerbations not requiring hospitalization and separated from each other based on symptoms, assessed using the Modified MRC Dyspnea Scale () or the CAT instrument, as follows: Group A: few symptoms (MRC score 0-1 or CAT score <10) and 0 to 1 exacerbations/year not leading to hospital admission. Group B: more symptoms (MRC >1 or CAT >10) and 0 to 1 exacerbations/year not leading to hospital admission.
Group E is not based on symptom score but on having 2 or more exacerbations/year and/or 1 or more exacerbations leading to hospitalization.
Smoking cessation is the cornerstone to therapy; reduction of exposure to risk factors such as air pollution and occupational dust and chemicals is also helpful.A

The goals for management of stable COPD are symptom relief and risk reduction.C The former includes improving exercise tolerance and health status and the latter includes preventing disease progression and reducing COPD exacerbations and mortality. Management of acute exacerbations is discussed in the chapter on COPD, acute exacerbation).

First-line therapy for initial COPD management is single or dual long-acting inhaled bronchodilator therapy (beta-agonist and/or anticholinergic).A GOLD 2024 recommends single bronchodilator treatment for those in Group A and combined LABA/LAMA for those in Groups B and E. The ATS recommends beginning with both types of agents (LABA/LAMA).A

Addition of inhaled glucocorticosteroid should be considered for patients with stage III or IV COPD with repeated exacerbations (GOLD Group E), particularly for those with high blood eosinophil counts, and in those with repeated exacerbations to reduce COPD exacerbations and mortality.B

Triple therapy with LAMA/LABA/ICS reduces moderate exacerbations in patients with stage III or IV moderate to severe COPD, especially if a recent exacerbation (NNT = 23 over one year), but the difference is small; most studies show no differences in severe exacerbations or mortality.A
GOLD 2024 notes that azithromycin can be considered in patients with continued exacerbations despite appropriate therapy, preferentially for smokers.B

In patients with severe to very severe airflow (FEV1 <50%), chronic bronchitis and exacerbations, GOLD 2024 recommends the addition of roflumilast, a phosphodiesterase 4 [PDE4] inhibitor, to long-acting bronchodilators with or without ICS can be considered.B
Exercise training programs and pulmonary rehabilitation programs improve exercise tolerance and reduce symptoms of dyspnea and fatigue.A

Supplemental oxygen (15-20 hours per day) has been shown to improve survival in patients with severe obstruction (resting PaO2 <55 mm Hg) and should be prescribed for patients with severe resting hypoxemia.A

See for an overview of therapy. Medications for most patients with COPD include bronchodilators (inhaled beta-2-adrenergic agonists and inhaled anticholinergics [LABA/LAMA] with addition of anti-inflammatory agents (inhaled and oral corticosteroids and azithromycin and/or roflumilast) and mucolytics if continued exacerbations occur despite inhaler therapy. Theophylline can be used if other medications are unavailable or unaffordable.

GOLD 2024 emphasizes the importance of education and training in inhaler device use including demonstration of proper technique and to recheck that patients are able to use their inhaler correctly at each visit.

The Canadian Thoracic Society (2023) differs somewhat in recommending initial triple inhaled therapy (LAMA/LABA/ICS) for those with a moderate/severe dyspnea and/or impaired health status and a high risk of exacerbations (Group E), with azithromycin, roflumilast or N-acetylcysteine recommended for specific populations. They recommend stepping up from LAMA or LABA to LAMA/LABA and then LAMA/LABA/ICS as the severity and the number of acute exacerbations increases. They recommend against the use of theophylline, maintenance systemic chronic oral corticosteroids such as prednisone, and treatment with an ICS alone for all patients with COPD.

listitem.strong: Stage I or GOLD Group A

list.listitem: A short- or long-acting inhaled bronchodilators can be used as needed for patients with infrequent episodes of dyspnea.

Long-acting (6-12-hour duration) beta 2-adrenergic agonists (LABAs) include arformoterol, bambuterol, clenbuterol, formoterol, salmeterol, and protokylol. Ultra-long acting (24-hour) agents include indacaterol, olodaterol, and vilanterol (in association with other drugs only).
Long-acting (12-24 hours duration) muscarinic antagonists (LAMAs) include tiotropium, aclidinium, umeclidinium, and glycopyrrolate (also called glycopyrronium).

Authors of a network meta-analysis of 40 studies comparing efficacy of long-acting bronchodilators in patients with COPD concluded that, with respect to trough FEV1 and Saint George Respiratory Questionnaire (SGRQ) score, indacaterol, glycopyrronium, and tiotropium were likely to be the most effective bronchodilators.

With respect to adverse effects (see below), authors of a retrospective cohort study based on a national insurance claims database of patients with COPD ≥40 years who were newly prescribed medication, the risk of severe adverse effects was lower among patients receiving umeclidinium/vilanterol or glycopyrrolate/indacaterol combinations compared to tiotropium/olodaterol; the incidence of cardiovascular events was similar across groups.

The choice of inhaler device should be individualized based on factors such as access, cost and ease of use and education on proper use provided. Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 19 studies found that adults with COPD preferred small inhaler devices that were portable, durable, perceived as easy to use, and delivered medication quickly. Instructions on inhaler technique should be given and repeated as needed.

Side effects of beta-2-adrenergic agonists include arrhythmias, hypokalemia, and hyperglycemia. While respiratory-related deaths and life-threatening experiences vs. placebo have been shown, primarily in asthma trials, authors of a recent evidence-based review found no convincing evidence that monotherapy with these agents in patients with COPD was associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular complications.

Side effects of anticholinergics include dry mouth, increased intraocular pressure, and urinary outlet obstruction. One meta-analysis demonstrated an increased risk of myocardial infarction (NNTH 174/year) and cardiovascular death (NNTH 40/year) but not all-cause mortality in patients with COPD using inhaled anticholinergic agents; use of these agents should be weighed against cardiac risk. Evidence, however, remains conflicting. According to the Medical Letter, Sept.7, 2020, data on the cardiovascular risks of LAMAs in patients with COPD show increased risk of cardiovascular events within meta-analyses and cohort studies, but not within individual RCTs.
GOLD 2024 recommends against using ICS as monotherapy in patients with stable COPD.

Authors of a Cochrane review of 55 studies with over 16,000 participants found ICS vs. placebo for patients with stable COPD were associated with significant benefits of reduced rate of exacerbations (MD -0.19 exacerbations per patient per year; 95%CI -0.30 to -0.08), reduced rate of decline in quality of life and possibly reduced rate of decline in FEV1. There was no mortality benefit. Potential side effects included oropharyngeal candidiasis, hoarseness, and increased risk of pneumonia (OR 1.56; 95% CI 1.30-1.86). Although not recommended as monotherapy, these authors support consideration of ICS in combination with long‐acting bronchodilators.

Side effects of ICS include oropharyngeal candidiasis and hoarseness are additional risk of pneumonia. ICS given in conventional doses to patients with mild COPD does not decrease bone mineral density or increase fracture risk. However, another systematic review concluded that use of ICS in older adults with COPD increased fracture risk somewhat (NNTH 83 over 3 years); this risk must be balanced against a NNT of 6 per year for preventing exacerbations.

listitem.strong: Stage II or GOLD Group B: Initial management

list.listitem: First-line initial therapy for patients in stage II or higher or GOLD Group B or higher is dual long-acting inhaled bronchodilator therapy (LABA/LAMA); the two classes of drugs are similarly effective.

An ATS review of 24 RCTs with 45,441 participants found improved symptom scores and reduced exacerbations and hospitalizations with combination LABA/LAMA compared to monotherapy without an increase in adverse events.

Combination LABA/LAMA in patients with stable COPD was also found to be better than placebo or monotherapy with either agent with respect to symptom indices based on a network meta-analysis of 23 RCTs with 27,172 patients. There were also fewer moderate-to-severe exacerbations with LABA/LAMA compared with LABAs alone but not LAMAs alone. Safety outcomes and number of severe exacerbations were similar between LABA/LAMA combinations and monotherapies. This was confirmed in a more recent network meta-analysis of 44 RCTs evaluating symptom scores (SGRQ) and use of recue medication in which LABA/LAMA combinations generally showed improved outcomes compared to placebo and monotherapy with tiotropium.

Authors of a Cochrane review concluded that combination LABA/LAMA was associated with a clinically significant improvement in lung function and health-related quality of life in patients with mild-to-moderate COPD compared to placebo.

Authors of a systematic review and network meta-analysis comparing different LABA/LAMA combinations found no strong evidence suggesting different benefits in terms of number of moderate-to-severe exacerbations or all-cause mortality among LAMA/LABAs in patients with stable COPD. Major adverse cardiovascular events and rates of pneumonia were also similar.

listitem.strong: Stage III or IV or GOLD E: Initial management

list.listitem: The 2024 GOLD and ATS recommendations are to begin with dual LABA/LAMA therapy. If further exacerbations occur, LABA/LAMA is preferred over LABA/ICS.

For patients whose symptoms are not controlled at follow-up, check inhaler technique and adherence and consider switching devices or molecules. Delivery devices include dry powder inhalers, inhalation spray inhalers, metered-dose inhalers and hydrofluoroalkane metered-dose inhalers. Information comparing these with respect to dose, cost and ease of use can be found in the Sept. 7, 2020 Medical Letter.
Addition of inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) to LABA/LAMA should be considered for patients with repeated exacerbations, particularly for those with high eosinophil counts (300 cells/μL or more).

ATS makes no recommendation for or against use of ICS in patients with eosinophilia because the 8 RCTs evaluated used post-hoc analyses that while suggesting improvements in exacerbations, dyspnea scores, and health-related quality of life increased risk of pneumonia.

In an RCT across 43 countries including 16,590 patients with COPD and an FEV1 between 50% and 70% of predicted, all-cause mortality was unaffected by combination fluticasone/vilanterol (the latter drug, an ultra-long acting beta-2 agonist) therapy or its components over placebo. All treatments reduced the rate of moderate and severe exacerbation and there were no reported excess risks of pneumonia over placebo (about 5%) or adverse cardiac events.

In a primary care study with 2269 patients comparing fluticasone/vilanterol with the patient's current usual care, slightly fewer exacerbations were observed in the intervention group (about 0.14 fewer per person per year, NNT = 7 to avoid one exacerbation per year), but there were trends toward more deaths (45 vs. 30) and deaths due to malignancy (13 vs. 3) in the treatment group.

In a 52-week drug-company-sponsored RCT of 3362 patients with COPD and a history of exacerbation during the previous year, combination inhaled LABA/LAMA was more effective than combination LABA/ICS in preventing COPD exacerbations (3.6 vs. 4.0; rate ratio 0.9, 95% CI 0.8-0.96) with similar side effects with the exception of reduced incidence of pneumonia (3.2 vs. 4.8%, respectively).

However, in a meta-analysis of 60 RCTs enrolling 103,034 patients inhaled therapy containing ICSs was associated with a reduction in all-cause mortality risk among patients with COPD compared with inhaled therapy without ICSs (Peto OR, 0.9; 95% CI, 0.8-0.97), especially triple therapy (Peto OR, 0.7; 95% CI, 0.6-0.9). Eosinophil counts of ≥200/μL (Peto OR, 0.6; 95% CI, 0.4-0.95) were the strongest predictor of this association. Other predictors included history of ≥2 moderate and severe exacerbations in the previous year, GOLD stages III or IV, age younger than 65 years, and BMI of ≥ 25 kg/m2.

For patients with continued exacerbations and a lower eosinophil count (<100 cells/μL), GOLD 2024 suggests addition of azithromycin in former smokers or roflumilast (a PDE4 inhibitor) in patients with chronic bronchitis and an FEV1 <50% of predicted as the third agent with LABA/LAMA or 4th agent, if the patients is already on triple therapy (see below for a discussion of these medications).

ATS has a conditional recommendation for addition of ICS to dual therapy in patients with ongoing dyspnea and exacerbation, and for the withdrawal of the ICS after 1 year in patients who do well. They based this recommendation on 4 RCTs with 9313 patients showing the addition of ICS to LABA/LAMA significantly reduced exacerbations (NNT = 16 for 1 fewer exacerbation), but had no clinical effect on symptom scores or health-related quality of life. Pneumonia occurred more frequently in patients treated with additional ICS in three of these studies (NNT to harm = 67).

Authors of a meta-analysis of 21 trials found that once daily triple therapy with LAMA/LABA/ICS reduced rates of moderate or severe exacerbations compared with LAMA monotherapy (rate ratio 0.7, 95% CI 0.6-0.9), LAMA/LABA (0.8, 0.7-0.9), and ICS/LABA (0.8, 0.7-0.9). Pneumonia risk was significantly higher with triple therapy than with LAMA/LABA (RR 1.5, 95% CI 1.3-1.9).

A reduction in exacerbations was also shown in a meta-analysis of 13 studies with 15,519 patients comparing LAMA/LABA/ICS with LABA/ICS which showed a RR of 0.8; 95% CI 0.7-0.9 and an NNT of 23 to prevent one exacerbation over a one-year period.

A retrospective cohort study found that after adjusting for differences between groups, all cause mortality was lower in patients taking triple therapy using a single inhaler compared with those using separate inhalers (HR = 0.82; 95% CI 0.75 - 0.91). It is possible that unmeasured confounding due to better healthcare access and higher income may be associated with both mortality and the ability to obtain the single inhaler therapy.

In an RCT of 8588 patients with moderate-severe COPD randomized to 1 of 4 regimens, those on triple therapy had a lower rate of moderate to severe exacerbations of 1.3 and 1.2 per year in the 320 mcg and 160 mcg triple therapy groups compared with 1.6 in the LAMA plus LABA group, and 1.5 in the ICS plus LABA (one fewer exacerbation every 4 years). There were no differences in mortality or severe adverse events at 1 year.

Triple therapy may also be associated with a slightly lower all-cause mortality than dual therapy with either LAMA/LABA or LABA/ICS based on a secondary analysis of the IMPACT study. This study enrolled 10,355 patients with severe COPD based on spirometry plus at least 1 moderate or severe exacerbation in the previous year OR with moderate COPD plus 2 or more moderately severe exacerbations or 1 severe exacerbation in the preceding year. After 1 year, 98 (2.4%) patients on triple therapy died compared with 109 (2.6%) patients who received LABA/ICS and 66 (3.2%) receiving LAMA/LABA.

In a 52-week RCT of triple therapy with different doses of ICS vs. dual combination therapy in 8509 patients with moderate-to-very-severe COPD and at least one exacerbation in the past year, those randomized to triple therapy with either steroid dose had a lower rate of moderate or severe COPD exacerbations. The adverse event rate was similar across the treatment groups (61.7%-64.5%) but the incidence of confirmed pneumonia was higher at 3.5% to 4.5% in the groups that included an ICS vs. 2.3% in the LABA/LAMA group.

In an RCT of 939 patients with COPD, a blood eosinophil count of at least 300/microliter and an elevated exacerbation risk despite use of standard triple therapy, those who were randomized to 300 mg dupilumab had 1 fewer moderate exacerbation about every 3 years (rate ratio 0.7, 95% CI 0.6 to 0.9), improved quality of life on the St. George's Respiratory Questionnaire, and less severe respiratory symptom scores on the Evaluating Respiratory Symptoms in COPD compared to those who received placebo. However, at a cost of $37,000 per year, dupilumab is not cost-effective.

A randomized trial identified 806 patients with eosinophilic asthma and at least 2 moderate or 1 severe exacerbation in the past year. Adding mepolizumab to standard triple therapy produced only a small reduction in moderate exacerbations, resulting to 1 fewer course of steroids and/or antibiotic every 5 years. It seems unlikely that this would be cost-effective given the high cost of monoclonal antibodies.
Systemic Glucocorticoids

Chronic treatment with systemic glucocorticosteroid should be avoided due to an unfavorable risk-benefit ratio. Concerns include diabetes, hypertension, osteoporosis, fracture, and cataracts, but the data are weak.

ATS makes conditional recommendations against use of oral steroids in patients with severe and frequent exacerbations based on their review of 11 studies, including 4 RCTs, which demonstrated no differences in mortality, exacerbations, hospitalizations, or dyspnea scores with oral steroids but a significant increase in the risk of adverse events.

The National Collaborating Center for Chronic Conditions recommends use of long-term (>15 hours daily) oxygen therapy for patients with a PaO2 greater than 7.3 but less than 8 KPa (<60 mm Hg) when stable and one of the following: secondary polycythemia, nocturnal hypoxemia (O2 saturation <90%), peripheral edema, or pulmonary hypertension. To benefit from oxygen therapy, supplemental oxygen should be used for at least 15 hours per day; greater benefit is seen in patients receiving oxygen for 20 hours per day.

GOLD 2024 guidelines note that long-term oxygen therapy improves survival in patients with severe resting hypoxemia and recommend long-term oxygen therapy for patients with a PaO2 at or below 7.3 kPa (55 mmHg) or SaO2 at or below 88%, with or without hypercapnia confirmed twice over a 3-week period; or PaO2 between 7.3 kPa (55 mmHg) and 8 kPa (60 mmHg) or SaO2 of 88%, with evidence of congestive heart failure or polycythemia.

The 2021 ATS guidelines on home oxygen recommend long-term home oxygen for at least 15 hours daily for patients with COPD and severe hypoxia defined as PaO2 at or below 7.3 kPa (55 mmHg) or SpO2 at or below 88% on pulse oximetry OR PaO2 between 7.5-7.9 kPa (56 and 59 mm Hg) or SpO2 at 89% for patients with COPD and edema, hematocrit of 55% or greater, or P pulmonale on electrocardiography.

ATS recommends against using home oxygen for patients with lower degrees of hypoxia. However, based on several lower-quality studies with conflicting data, the ATS recommends use of ambulatory oxygen in patients with COPD who develop severe exertional hypoxia on room air (SpO2 88% or lower) and for those who desaturate during exertion. They also recommend using liquid oxygen for ambulatory patients who need higher oxygen flow rate.

The British Thoracic Society also recommends oxygen therapy for patients with stable COPD with a resting PaO2 ≤8 kPa with evidence of peripheral edema, polycythemia (hematocrit ≥55%) or pulmonary hypertension. They also recommend long-term oxygen for patients with resting hypercapnia provided they meet other criteria for its use. Patients being assessed for long-term oxygen therapy should not be assessed using pulse oximetry alone.

Authors of a Cochrane review found low-quality evidence that supplemental oxygen reduces breathlessness in patients with mild or no hypoxemia, even if it does not reduce mortality (32 studies; 865 participants); short-burst oxygen given before exercise was not of benefit.

In one small trial, supplemental oxygen therapy for patients with normal resting O2 saturation but desaturation with exertion was not shown to improve quality of life, although walking endurance was somewhat improved (2.5 minutes).In another study of supplemental oxygen during walking, patients with resting hypoxemia or exercise-induced hypoxemia significantly increased 6-minute walk distance, although less than half of patients reached the threshold of a clinically-relevant improvement.

In a time-to-event analysis of an RCT including 738 patients with stable COPD and resting or exercise-induced moderate desaturation comparing supplemental oxygen to no supplemental oxygen, no differences were found after 18 months in time to death or first hospitalization (HR 0.94, 95% CI 0.79-1.12) or in rates of hospitalizations or COPD exacerbations between groups. There were also no consistent between-group differences in measures of quality of life, lung function, or 6-minute walking distance. More adverse events were noted in the oxygen group, including lots of tripping over equipment and one fire.

In one study of 116 patients with severe COPD admitted for an exacerbation who required non-invasive ventilation (NIV) in the hospital, and had persistent hypercapnia and hypoxemia 2 to 4 weeks after achieving clinical stability, those randomized to home NIV and oxygen had fewer subsequent readmissions and better quality of life, although no difference in mortality.

In a small randomized cross-over trial of 12 patients with severe COPD and baseline hypercapnia on long-term oxygen therapy, those randomized to automatically-titrated O2 flows, termed FreeO2, had improved exercise endurance and oxygen saturation compared to constant flow O2.

In another study, use of FreeO2 improved time spent at target O2 saturation by 56.3% and was found likely to be cost effective with a savings of 20.7% of the per-patient costs at 180 days; however, this difference did not reach significance.

In an RCT of 137 patients with COPD and chronic hypoxemia, the addition of high-flow oxygen vs. Venturi mask provided no additional benefit on improving endurance time, the primary outcome, but was minimally more effective in improving walking distance.

High-flow oxygen delivered via nasal cannula compared to standard oxygen delivery, however, significantly reduced the rate of moderate/severe exacerbations (unadjusted mean count 1.0 vs. 2.5) and improved health-related quality of life scores and peripheral oxygen saturation daytime in patients with hypercapnia and GOLD stages 2-4 receiving long-term oxygen therapy.

Routine use of antibiotic courses outside of exacerbations is not recommended. For patients with continued exacerbations and a lower eosinophil count (<100 cells/mL), GOLD 2024 suggests addition of azithromycin in former smokers as the third agent with LABA/LAMA or 4th agent if the patients is already on triple therapy. GOLD 2024 notes that there are no data showing benefit or safety of chronic azithromycin treatment to prevent COPD exacerbations beyond one-year of treatment. They recommend consideration of azithromycin in former smokers with exacerbations despite appropriate therapy.

Prophylactic antibiotics in patients with chronic bronchitis/COPD has a small but statistically significant effect in reducing the days of illness due to exacerbations of chronic bronchitis but not a significant reduction in number of exacerbations. Risks include antibiotic resistance and adverse drug effects, especially hearing.
A Dutch trial found that the tertile of patients who respond best to azithromycin have more respiratory symptoms, higher WBC count, lower hemoglobin, higher C-reactive protein and lower FVC.

In a Cochrane review examining different prophylactic antibiotics on exacerbations, quality of life, and serious adverse events in people with COPD in three separate network meta-analyses, authors found prolonged administration of macrolides vs. placebo appeared beneficial in prolonging the time to next exacerbation, improving quality of life, and reducing serious adverse events. No clear benefits were associated with use of quinolones or tetracyclines. Antibiotic resistance could not be thoroughly and none of the eligible studies excluded patients with previously isolated non-tuberculous mycobacteria, which would contraindicate prophylactic administration of antibiotics.
In an RCT including 222 patients with moderate to severe COPD and an exacerbation history, once-daily doxycycline for 1 year was no better than placebo at decreasing exacerbations.

While one RCT found daily azithromycin reduced exacerbations (0.34 fewer exacerbations per year) and slightly reduced hospitalizations for COPD, azithromycin did not change the total number of hospitalizations and increased cost by approximately $1200 per year. Patients most likely to respond to daily azithromycin include those who are older, have a milder GOLD stage and are not current smokers.

In one small trial, daily antibiotic use for 13 weeks did not significantly reduce total airway bacterial load but increased bacterial resistance; mean inhibitory concentrations of cultured isolates increased by at least three times over placebo.

GOLD 2024 guidelines recommend consideration of adding romflumilast to long-acting bronchodilator therapy with or without ICS in patients with severe to very-severe airflow limitation, chronic bronchitis and exacerbations.

Authors of a Cochrane review of oral phosphodiesterase 4 [PDE4] inhibitors, roflumilast and cilomilast found benefit over placebo in improving lung function and reducing likelihood of exacerbations, but little impact on quality of life.Benefit for reducing exacerbations and hospital admissions was also seen in the most recent trial. These agents are proposed to reduce the airway inflammation and bronchoconstriction in COPD. The optimum place of PDE4 inhibitors in COPD management is unclear.

In one short-term (4 week) RCT of sildenafil administration to patients with COPD but without pulmonary hypertension, sildenafil had no beneficial effect on exercise capacity and significantly worsened gas exchange at rest and quality of life.

Adverse drug effects: primarily gastrointestinal (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, increased gastric acid secretion), headache, unexplained weight loss, and sleeplessness. There are also concerns about psychiatric adverse events with roflumilast.
Patients with alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency can be treated with infusion of purified alpha-1 antitrypsin in addition to usual treatments.

Cardioselective beta-blockers given to patients with COPD who have indications for this drug class (eg, hypertension, heart failure, coronary artery disease) were not found to cause adverse respiratory effects in a Cochrane review. However, a trial randomized 532 adults age 40-85 with moderate to severe COPD to long-acting metoprolol or placebo. There was no difference in the number of exacerbations but those in the metoprolol group did have a higher risk of hospitalization for an exacerbation (HR 1.9, 95% CI 1.3 to 2.8).

Oral theophylline has a modest positive effect on lung function and likely exercise performance in patients with moderate-to-severe COPD; it can be considered if inhaled bronchodilators are unavailable or ineffective as an added or alternative agent.

In an RCT of 1578 patients with COPD at high risk for exacerbation, the addition of theophylline 200 mg once or twice daily conferred no benefit on any outcome measures. The 2024 Canadian guidelines recommend against theophylline for patients with COPD.

Mucolytics (eg, guaifenesin) are associated with a small reduction in acute exacerbations, reduced total days of disability, and possibly reduced hospitalizations. They should be considered in patients in Group E not currently on inhaled steroids, especially in winter time.

Use of N-acetylcysteine (600 milligrams twice daily) in patients with stable COPD is associated with a reduction in COPD exacerbations (1.0 vs. 1.7 times yearly). Authors of a meta-analysis of 9 RCTs including 2137 patients with COPD did not find benefit of N-acetylcysteine vs. placebo on risk of acute exacerbation or symptom score.

P38 mitogen-activated protein kinase inhibitors are anti-inflammatory agents under investigation for use in patients with COPD as well as other chronic diseases. In one RCT, a once-daily oral form was improved trough FEV1 and baseline dyspnea in patients with moderate to severe COPD. However, side effects including liver toxicity and skin reactions limit have been problematic. Inhaled agents, under development, will likely to improve the therapeutic window between efficacy and adverse events. Long-term efficacy is unknown.

Interleukin-5 receptor alpha-directed cytolytic monoclonal antibody: In a report of two RCT comparing several doses of add-on benralizumab vs. usual care in patients with COPD who had frequent exacerbations despite receiving guideline-based inhaled treatment, there was no difference in annualized rate of COPD exacerbations regardless of eosinophil count.
Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors such as acetazolamide, which is used for mountain sickness, can produce small increases in arterial PO2 and decrease in PCO2 but clinical benefit has not been shown.
In an RCT of 380 patients undergoing mechanical ventilation for COPD exacerbation, acetazolamide afforded no improvement in respiratory parameters.

Authors of a Cochrane review of 4 small trials with a total of 84 patients with advanced COPD concluded that acetazolamide produced a small increase in arterial PO2 and fall in PCO2 that was of uncertain clinical benefit.

Authors of a review of 4 studies with 504 patients with COPD, obesity hypoventilation syndrome or obstructive sleep apnea who were hospitalized with acute respiratory deterioration complicated by metabolic alkalosis found no benefit of acetazolamide on mortality or duration of ventilatory support.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 10 trials with 1,471 patients found that statin treatment was associated with a larger improvement in exercise capacity, lung function, and St. George's Respiratory Questionnaire score vs. placebo, but there were no statistically significant differences in all-cause mortality.

In another meta-analysis of noncardiovascular disease benefits or risks of statins, authors concluded that statins decreased exacerbations in patients with COPD although benefits were not likely large enough to be clinically relevant. A mortality benefit was reported in a meta-analysis conducted by Chinese authors of RR 0.72, 95% CI 0.63-0.84 in addition to a reduction in COPD exacerbations.
Gabapentinoids are associated with an increased risk of severe exacerbations (death or hospitalization, hazard ratio 1.39, 95% CI 1.29-1.50).
A study randomized 519 adults with COPD to bisoprolol 1.25 mg daily titrated to 5 mg daily or placebo. After 2 years there was no difference in COPD exacerbations, hospitalizations, or mortality.
LVRS is a surgical procedure involving removal of parts of the lungs to reduce hyperinflation and improve mechanical efficiency.

GOLD 2024 notes that LVRS improves survival for patients with severe upper-lobe emphysema and low post-rehabilitation exercise capacity; health status and quality of life improve even for those with high post-rehabilitation exercise capacity. They note that LVRS is associated with higher mortality in those with severe COPD with an FEV1 <20% and either homogeneous emphysema on CT or diffusion lung capacity of <20% predicted.

The National Collaborating Center for Chronic Conditions recommend consideration for LVRS for patients who remain breathless with significant reductions in activities of daily living despite maximal therapy if they have an FEV1 greater than 20% predicted, PaCO2 less than 7.3 kPa, upper lobe emphysema, and transfer factor for carbon monoxide of more than 20% predicted.

Authors of a Cochrane review of 1 large and 10 small studies found that LVRS for patients with severe diffuse emphysema increased 90-day mortality (OR 6.2; 95% CI 3.2-12). In those who survived, however, there was improvement in quality of life and exercise capacity. Outcomes were more favorable for those with upper lobe-predominant emphysema with low exercise capacity.
In another RCT using a composite endpoint of quality of life and death, LVRS increased the time to the composite endpoint by 1 year.
LVRS is associated with a reduction in mean blood pressure.

Lung transplantation has been shown in selected patients with severe COPD to improve quality of life and function, but not survival. GOLD 2023 indications for consideration of lung transplant are progressive disease despite maximal medical treatment, not candidates for lung volume reduction surgery, have a BODE index of 5 to 6, a PaCO2 > 50 mmHg (6.6 kPa) and/or PaO2 < 60 mmHg (8 kPa) and FEV1 < 25%. They should be considered for listing for lung transplantation when the BODE index is >7, FEV1 is <15 to 20%, and they have had three or more severe exacerbations during the previous year, one severe exacerbation with hypercapnic respiratory failure, or have moderate to severe pulmonary hypertension.

According to data from the International Society for Heart and Lung Transplantation, one-year survival for adult lung-transplant patients is about 80% to 85% and 70% of those who survive to one year are alive at 5 years.
Major complications of lung transplantation include acute rejection, bronchiolitis obliterans, opportunistic infections and lymphoproliferative disease.

An endobronchial valve is an implanted device that promotes one-way airflow to empty the lungs preventing air trapping. Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 8 prospective trails with 744 patients with advanced COPD concluded that there was benefit with respect to lung function and disease-specific quality of life.

TLD is bronchoscopic radiofrequency ablation therapy intended to disrupt parasympathetic pulmonary nerves thereby decreasing airway resistance and mucus hypersecretion. In an RCT of 82 patients, mean age 63.7 years, with symptomatic moderate-severe COPD despite pharmacotherapy, TLD compared to sham TLD resulted in fewer COPD exacerbations requiring hospitalization in the 0- to 12.5-month window (hazard ratio 0.35; 95% CI 0.13-0.99) although there was no statistical difference in the time to first moderate-severe COPD exacerbation or patient-reported symptoms over the 12.5 month period. However, during the predefined 3- to 6.5-month window, patients in the TLD group experienced significantly fewer respiratory adverse events vs. the sham group (32% vs. 71%). Respiratory adverse events were defined as COPD exacerbation, tachypnea, wheezing, worsening bronchitis, worsening dyspnea, influenza, pneumonia, other respiratory infections, respiratory failure, or airway effects requiring therapeutic intervention.
Use of immunostimulant therapy containing bacterial extracts reduced hospital days (1.5 days on average vs. 3.4 days) in patients with COPD in 1 RCT.

In one RCT, the addition of Cineole from eucalyptus oil at 200 mg three times daily reduced severity and duration of exacerbations and improved lung function, dyspnea, and quality of life in patients with stable COPD.

Ginseng as an adjunct to pharmacotherapy may be of some benefit on lung function and quality of life, but data are of low quality. In the most recent 12-month RCT of 168 patients with moderate COPD, there was no significant difference in improvement in health-related quality of life between ginseng and the placebo group; both groups showed symptomatic improvement.

Chinese herbal medicine as an adjunct to LABA/ICS improves St. George's Respiratory Questionnaire scores and increases FEV1. Runfeijianpibushen decoction and Renshenbufei pills appears to perform best. In another RCT of 60 patients with stable COPD who were taking inhaled steroids and bronchodilators, those randomized to the Chinese herb formula Yufeining vs. placebo had improved CAT scores and mMRC grades in addition to increased six-minute walking distance.
