In a Chinese RCT of 40 patients with stable COPD, use of Compound Caoshi silkworm granules vs. standard treatment improved symptoms at 3 months but there was no difference in objective measures.

Tai Chi Qigong performed twice weekly in 60 minute sessions was significantly better than exercise or no intervention on exercise tolerance and 3-month exacerbation rate in patients with COPD. In another RCT, Liuzijue qigong plus daily walking for 6 months improved functional capacity and several quality-of-life measures over vs. daily walking alone in older adults with COPD.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 6 RCTs concluded that Qigong training improved self-reported depression and anxiety, 6-minute walk test distance (mean difference 39.31, 95% CI 18.27-60.34) and St. George's Respiratory Questionnaire total score.

In an RCT comparing traditional acupuncture with placebo needling, acupuncture reduced dyspnea from baseline based on the Borg scale score after the 6-minute walk test. In a second RCT, real vs. sham acupuncture confirmed benefit on exertional dyspnea and health-related quality of life after 8 weeks of treatment.
Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 12 studies with 798 participants concluded that body acupuncture improved health-related quality of life in patients with COPD.

A 4-month treatment with Bu-Fei Yi-Shen granule combined with acupoint sticking therapy vs. placebo granule and placebo sticking therapy for patients with stable COPD (both groups also on theophylline) showed beneficial effects on frequency and duration of acute exacerbation, symptoms, and six-minute walking distance at 6-month follow-up.

listitem.strong: Noninvasive positive pressure ventilation as home therapy

list.listitem: GOLD 2024 guidelines recommend consideration of long-term non-invasive ventilation in selected patients, particularly those with pronounced daytime hypercapnia and recent hospitalization, although evidence is lacking. In patients with both COPD and obstructive sleep apnea, continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) is indicated.

Authors of a meta-analysis of data from patients with COPD and hypercapnia found use of home NIPPV via bilevel positive airway pressure, compared with no device, was associated with a lower mortality risk (22.31% vs 28.57%; OR 0.66; 95% CI 0.51-0.87; 13 studies with 1423 patients); all-cause hospital admission was reduced based on a single study (39.74% vs 75.00%; OR, 0.22; 95% CI 0.11-0.43) and there was reduced incidence of intubation based on 3 studies (5.34% vs 14.71%; OR 0.34; 95% CI 0.14-0.83). There was no significant difference in quality of life. Use of home mechanical ventilator devices, however, was not associated with reduced mortality although their use reduced all-cause hospital admissions based on a single study (rate ratio 0.50; 95% CI 0.35-0.71). All studies were at high risk of bias.

Oscillatory positive expiratory pressure (OPEP) devices are intended to facilitate sputum clearance and reduce cough. In an RCT enrolling 122 patients with COPD, daily or most-day sputum production, and FEV1 25-56% predicted, those randomized to 3 months of OPEP had significantly reduced cough as measured by the Leicester Cough Questionnaire, reduced cough frequency, and improved fatigue and quality of life but no improvement in sleep disturbance.
Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis found exercise interventions lead to improved exercise tolerance and health-related quality of life even in patients with very severe COPD.

Authors of a Cochrane review found evidence of improved physical activity with exercise training, physical activity counseling and COPD medications. The optimal timing and duration of interventions is unclear.

Exercise training for 12 months following pulmonary rehabilitation improved exercise capacity (1-min sit-to-stand-test) and patient-perceived fitness but had no influence on dyspnea in an RCT including 123 patients with COPD (of whom 104 completed follow-up).

Engaging in moderate to vigorous physical activity following the diagnosis of COPD was associated with reduced mortality (adjusted HR 0.8, 95% CI 0.8-0.9) and reduced severe exacerbations (adjusted HR 0.9, 95% CI, 0.87-0.94) compared to a group that did not engage in exercise.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 34 RCTs with 2456 patients found total mind-body movement therapy (TMBM) more effective than exercise-based cardiopulmonary rehabilitation for improvement in 6-minute walk distance in patients with COPD. Use of adjunctive TMBM to exercise therapy improved both quality of life and 6-minute walk distance in patients with COPD compared to exercise therapy alone.

An RCT with 436 adults with chronic respiratory disease found that pulmonary rehabilitation is similarly effective when performed using minimal equipment (eg, timed walking circuit, body weight exercises, steppers, and elastic resistance bands) or using gym-based equipment (eg, treadmills, cycle ergometers, fixed weight machine, and free weights). Thus, inaccessibility for various reasons to specialist gym-based exercise equipment should not be a barrier to this beneficial intervention.

GOLD 2024 recommends PR as essential for patients with COPD in Groups B and E, and notes that optimum benefits are achieved from programs lasting 6 to 8 weeks. Caution should be used for hospitalized patients as initiating PR before discharge may reduce 1-year survival.

The American Thoracic Society (2023) also make recommendations for pulmonary rehabilitation for adults with stable COPD (moderate-quality evidence) and after hospitalization for COPD exacerbation (moderate-quality evidence).

PR improves dyspnea, fatigue, and emotional function and increases patients' sense of control over their condition, health-related quality of life and exercise capacity. Authors of a Cochrane review of 9 RCTs found use of PR following an exacerbation of COPD reduced hospital admissions (pooled OR 0.22, 95% CI 0.08-0.58; NNT 4 over 25 weeks) and mortality (OR 0.28, 95% CI 0.10-0.84; NNT 6 over 107 weeks).

In addition, investigators using a database of Medicare beneficiaries found that initiation of PR within 90 days of hospitalization for a COPD exacerbation was associated with improved 1-year survival compared with initiation after 90 days or not at all. Unfortunately, few patients were enrolled in PR.
Both PR and exercise interventions appear to reduce functional decline as measured by 6-minute walking distance in patients who experienced a COPD exacerbation, based on a meta-analysis of RCTs.
In an RCT of 196 hospitalized patients with a COPD exacerbation, use of an educational video did not increase PR uptake within 28 days of hospital discharge.

In a 3-year RCT of maintenance PR in 138 patients with moderate to severe COPD, a beneficial effect was observed on BODE index and 6-minute walking distance at 2-years compared with a standard strategy, but this effect was no longer evident after the second year of follow-up.

In a 6-month RCT completed by 60 participants, use of a smartphone application (Kaia COPD) which provided a comprehensive training program improved COPD symptoms compared to the control group, but did not significantly improve the primary outcome of daily steps.

In a Cochrane review of nonpharmacologic interventions for advanced COPD, breathing training, walking aids, neuroelectrical muscle stimulation, and chest wall vibration appeared effective in reducing breathlessness.

Smoking cessation is the cornerstone to therapy. In 1 RCT of smoking cessation in patients with asymptomatic airway obstruction, all-cause mortality was lower in the group receiving smoking intervention. The effectiveness of e-cigarettes as an aid to smoking cessation is uncertain.

Limited evidence shows that combination psychosocial and pharmacologic interventions are more effective than no treatment to achieve smoking cessation. See GOLD 2024 for additional information on smoking cessation pharmacotherapy.

GOLD 2024 guidelines recommend self-management education with case manager support with or without a written action plan; action plans should target dyspnea management and prevention of exacerbations.

Self-management education versus usual care reduces the possibility of at least one hospital admission within 1 year; NNT of 10 (range 6-35) for patients with a 51% risk of exacerbation and NNT of 24 (range 16-80) for patients with a 13% risk of exacerbation. However, in a recent RCT, education and supported self-management for patients with moderate to severe COPD did not result in fewer deaths or hospital admissions over the course of a year. In another RCT of 165 patients with COPD, neither patient self-management, including an individualized action plan, nor case-manager monitoring produced positive changes in quality of life, number of exacerbations, or patients' reports of self-efficacy over usual care.

Telephone health coaching delivered by trained nurses in four sessions over 11 weeks in 289 primary care patients with mild symptoms of dyspnea vs. 288 usual-care patients led to changes in self-management activities, but did not improve health-related quality of life.

In an evidence review, authors concluded that there was little evidence of benefit of providing self-management support to patients shortly after hospital discharge, although there might be a reduction in hospital admissions and improvement in health-related quality of life.

However, in a single institution RCT of 240 patients hospitalized for COPD, those randomized to a comprehensive 3-month self-management program including family caregivers delivered by trained COPD nurses plus 30-day transition support compared to transition support alone had significantly fewer emergency department visits, COPD-related hospitalizations (135 vs. 202, respectively) and better health-related quality of life (St George's Respiratory Questionnaire score -1.53 vs. 5.44, respectively) at 6 months after discharge.

This study is in contrast to the most recent single-center RCT of a 3-month program of nurse-supported COPD self-management delivered to patients hospitalized due to COPD. In this study, the 120 patients randomized to the intervention had significantly more COPD-related hospitalizations and emergency department visits than the usual care group, without improvement in symptom scores or quality of life.

Training primary care providers to deliver an integrated disease management approach to patients with COPD showed no benefit over usual care on health outcomes. Similarly, protocol-based care management delivered by medical assistants did not reduce all-cause hospitalizations. There were some positive effects on quality of life measures at a cost of $10 per patient per month.
Nursing outreach programs improve disease-specific health-related quality of life but data on their impact on hospitalization rates are conflicting.
Use of a clinical pathway for COPD reduced complications, readmissions, and hospital length of stay but did not influence mortality or quality of life.

Nutritional support does not appear to improve anthropomorphic measures or function in patients with stable COPD. However, a more recent systematic review of 13 small trials found nutritional support (primarily oral supplements) improved total intake, body weight (about 2 kg), and grip strength (mean improvement 5.3%) in patients with COPD. GOLD guidelines state that nutritional support should be considered in malnourished patients with COPD.

Use of an indoor portable high-efficiency particulate air cleaner for 6 months compared to a sham device for former smokers with moderate-to-severe COPD reduced moderate exacerbations (incidence rate ratio, 0.3 [95% CI, 0.1-0.9]) and rescue medication use in an RCT including 116 subjects, although there was no significant improvement in overall SGRQ symptom scores. There was a significant improvement in the SGRO subscale for Breathlessness, Cough, and Sputum.

Use of energy conservation (prescribe rest periods, in this case 5 seconds every 3 steps) vs. stair climbing at the patient’s own pace, was helpful in reducing dyspnea during stair climbing in an RCT of 22 patients with severe COPD.

Limited evidence supports use of cognitive behavioral therapy for treating COPD-related depression. However, in an RCT including 423 patients with moderate/very severe COPD and mild/moderate anxiety and/or depression enrolled in pulmonary rehabilitation, randomization to six to eight 40- to 60-minute sessions plus telephone support throughout pulmonary rehabilitation was neither clinically effective nor cost-effective with respect to the primary outcomes of anxiety or depression or secondary outcomes of health-related quality of life, smoking status, uptake of pulmonary rehabilitation or healthcare use.
In a small Chinese RCT, group singing therapy reduced depressive symptoms and improved quality of life in patients with stable COPD.

Authors of a Cochrane review of 10 RCTs of “telehealthcare” (healthcare provided at a distance through communication from the patient to the health care provider who then responds with management feedback) concluded that such care was associated with a clinically significant increase in quality of life and possibly a reduction in the number of times patients attended the emergency department and the hospital.

In another systematic review and meta-analysis of 27 papers, tele-monitoring of patients with COPD reduced emergency room visits (risk ratio 0.63, 95% CI 0.55-0.72) and hospitalizations (risk ratio 0.88, 95% CI 0.80-0.97).

Data are not uniformly positive. In one RCT of 256 patients with a history of admission for exacerbations of COPD, telemonitoring was not effective in postponing admissions or improving quality of life over usual care.

With respect to telerehabilitation, GOLD 2024 notes that the evidence base is still evolving and best practices are not yet established. The most recent 2-year RCT of telerehabilitation, consisting of individualized treadmill training at home supervised by a physiotherapist and self-management, found that both telerehabilitation and unsupervised treadmill training at home were successful in reducing hospital readmissions and emergency department visits compared to a control group (1.2 events per person-year; 95% CI 0.9-1.5, 1.1; 95% CI, 0.9-1.4, and 1.9; 95% CI, 1.6-2.2, respectively).

Telecare provided by a nurse and social worker palliative care team for adults at high risk of death who had poor quality of life, produced clinically meaningful improvements in quality-of-life scores at 6 months compared with usual care in an RCT including 177 patients with COPD. The program involved 6 phone calls with a nurse to help with symptom management and 6 phone calls with a social worker to provide psychosocial care.

More than 80% of patients with an exacerbation can be manage as outpatients. The GOLD 2024 guideline recommends hospital assessment for patients with severe symptoms (worsening resting dyspnea, confusion), acute respiratory failure, severe underlying COPD, onset of new physical signs (cyanosis, peripheral edema), presence of serious comorbidities, (eg, heart failure, new arrhythmia), or insufficient home support.

In one non-inferiority RCT of 118 patients presenting to the hospital with a COPD exacerbation and DECAF score of 0-1, there were no differences in health outcomes or readmissions between those randomized to home vs. hospital care (mean length of stay 3 days). Home care was preferred by most and resulted in cost savings.

The use of discharge bundles, a set of evidence-based practices aimed at improving patient outcomes after discharge, appears to reduce rehospitalization but does not influence mortality of improve quality of life based on a systematic review of 14 studies, including 5 RCTs.

A health system-level intervention that delivered proactive specialty supported care to 365 primary care providers following discharge of their 352 patients improved patient’s quality of life but did not reduce 180-day readmission or death. Of 519 recommendations made, 401 (77.3%) were endorsed.
Consider referral for patients with frequent exacerbations, new onset arrhythmia, diagnostic uncertainty, and older age.

Consider referral to hospice for patients with very advanced or terminal illness. GOLD 2024 guidelines recommend advance care planning and end-of-life discussions with patients with COPD. This is especially important in patients with poor prognosis such as those with disabling dyspnea at rest that is poorly responsive to bronchodilators or with progression of advanced disease demonstrated by increasing hospitalizations or emergency department visits.
Elements of palliative care that can reduce symptoms include opiates, oxygen, nutritional support, and mind-body interventions.

GOLD 2024 guidelines suggest that low-dose long-acting oral or parenteral opioids may be considered for treating dyspnea in patients with COPD and severe disease. Additional research is needed on which patient characteristics predict response to opioid therapy, and the optimal formulation and administration route is unknown.

ATS also makes conditional recommendations for using opioids in patients with advanced refractory dyspnea despite optimal therapy based on 14 small RCTs with 366 patients showing improved health-related quality of life and dyspnea scores with opiates.

However, in an RCT of 156 people with COPD and severe chronic breathlessness, daily low-dose, extended-release morphine did not significantly reduce the intensity of worst breathlessness after 1 week of treatment.
Acute exacerbation of COPD is discussed in another chapter; antibiotics may reduce short-term mortality. A 5-day course of antibiotics is likely sufficient.

Symptoms such as fatigue, weight loss and anorexia can occur in patients with severe COPD and may have prognostic importance. Depression and anxiety are also common symptoms and should be identified and addressed.
Based on 14 trials of patients with respiratory failure due to acute exacerbation of COPD, NIPPV decreased mortality (RR 0.52; 95% CI 0.35-76), need for intubation, and treatment failure.

Authors of a Cochrane review concluded that an NIPPV strategy versus an invasive PPV strategy reduced mortality, intensive care unit and hospital length of stay, and duration of mechanical support; there were insufficient data to assess quality of life.

NIPPV as a weaning strategy for patients on ventilators for respiratory failure reduces rates of death and pneumonia without increasing the risk of weaning failure or re-intubation for patients with COPD.

In a small RCT, NIPPV was no better than usual care in reducing reintubation or hospital stay in patients with severe COPD immediately following extubation; small numbers may have precluded finding a clinically important difference.

For patients with COPD on a ventilator, bronchoscopic sputum suction compared to general sputum suction resulted in a shorter time of invasive ventilation, total time of ventilation and hospital stay; a lower reintubation rate, ventilator-associated pneumonia incidence and fatality rate; and a higher weaning success rate.
Cases of invasive pulmonary aspergillosis with a high mortality rate (91%) have been reported; most patients have severe COPD and/or history of corticosteroid use.

Patients with COPD are at increased risk of herpes zoster (adjusted HR 1.68; 95% CI 1.45-1.95); risk increases with use of inhaled steroids (adjusted HR 2.09; 95% CI 1.38-3.16) and oral steroids (adjusted HR 3.00; 95% CI 2.40-3.75).

Patients with COPD who have airway bacterial colonization appear to have more frequent COPD exacerbations and higher levels of both airway and systemic inflammation. This COPD subgroup is also considered at increased risk of developing cardiovascular complications.

Coronavirus (COVID)-19: It is not known whether patients with COPD are more susceptible to COVID-19 but, thus far, it does not seem to be an independent risk factor for infection. In fact, patients with COPD appear to be underrepresented among patients with COVID-19 perhaps due to use of ICS which decreases angiotensin-converting enzyme expression and may reduce viral entry.

Data are conflicting about whether COPD is an independent risk factor for hospitalization from COVID-19. Hospitalization rates for patients with COPD and COVID-19 range from 2% in a Shanghai cohort to 17.7% of hospitalized patients in the UK. However, patients with COPD are overrepresented among those with severe illness requiring intensive care.

The GOLD 2024 includes a chapter about COPD and COVID-19 infection (created in 2021). They recommend no need to change current COPD medications, testing for COVID-19 in patients with COPD who present with worsening respiratory symptoms accompanied by fever and/or any COVID-related symptoms, and restricting spirometry to patients requiring urgent or essential tests for COPD diagnosis and/or to assess lung function status for interventional procedures or surgery. Other advice is similar for patients with and without COPD. A printable checklist and guidance for phone/virtual follow-up with patients with COPD is provided.

The Center for Disease Control and Prevention report that age-adjusted death rates from COPD in the US have decreased since 1999 from 123.9/100,000 to 105.6/100,000 in 2019. Death rates are higher for men than women (116.2/100,000 and 98/100,000, respectively).
In a longitudinal study of 227 patients with COPD in Japan, 5-year survival was 73%; level of dyspnea and not FEV1 was correlated with survival rates.

In a database study of 339,647 people with COPD in England who were alive between January 2010 and January 2020, 97,882 (29%) died during follow-up. About one quarter (25.7%) of the deaths were COPD-related and 23.3% were cardiovascular-disease related. Airflow limitation, GOLD group, exacerbation frequency and severity, and COPD phenotype were associated with all-cause mortality.

Because patients with severe COPD have a poor 5-year survival, end-of-life care conversations should be conducted. In one RCT, despite an initial increase in end-of-life communication using a patient feedback form, the intervention did not increase documentation of subsequent conversations about end-of-life care, which occurred in about three quarters of patients, or improve documentation of advance directives, present for about one quarter of patients.

The BODE index (body mass index, degree of airflow obstruction, dyspnea, and exercise capacity) can be used to predict risk of hospitalization and death in patients with COPD.B In one population study, the BODE index had better survival prediction than the GOLD categories A-D (area under the curve 0.71 vs. 0.68, respectively). Adding the Copd cO-morbidity TEst (COTE) to the BODE index significantly improved outcome prediction (area under the curve 0.81). However, in a Taiwanese study, GOLD classification performed better than BODE in identifying individuals at risk of exacerbations; both indices were poor at predicting mortality in elderly adults with COPD.

The DECAF score (Dyspenia, Eosinopenia, Consolidation, Acidemia, and atrial Fibrillation). A DECAF score of 0 to 1 identified low-risk patients who might be suitable for home care or early supported discharge and a DECAF score of 3-6 identified high-risk patients who might be appropriate for more aggressive or palliative care.
In one study of 9047 patients, CT evidence of emphysema (identified in 29%) was a significant predictor of death from COPD (HR 9.3; 95% CI 4.3-20.2) and from lung cancer (HR 1.7; 95% CI 1.1-2.5).
Other clinical predictors of exacerbation include comorbid physician-diagnosed asthma and the modified Medical Research Council dyspnea score.
Chronic weight loss is also a predictor of mortality.
Authors of a meta-analysis of 9 studies found that a high neutrophil to lymphocyte ratio predicted risk of exacerbation (OR 3.81, 95% CI 1.20-12.13) and mortality (OR 2.60, 95% CI 1.48-4.57).

In another small study of 138 patients with COPD and depression admitted for inpatient rehabilitation, 1-year all-cause mortality was 22%. Risk factors for mortality were recent falls and dyspnea during activities.

Pneumonia: In a population study of 40,414 adults with COPD followed for 10 years, 8% experienced community-acquired pneumonia (incidence rate 22.4 [95% CI 21.7-23.2] per 1000 person years). Risk factors on multivariate modeling included age >65 years, congestive heart failure, dementia, prior severe COPD exacerbations requiring hospitalization and severe COPD requiring home oxygen or nebulized therapy. An observational study found that use of inhaled corticosteroids may also increase the risk of pneumonia.

Hospitalization: Exposure to fine ambient particulate matter (each 10-μg/m3 increment) is associated with a 3.1% (95% CI 1.6%-4.6%) increase in COPD hospitalizations and a 2.5% (95% CI 1.5%-3.5%) increase in COPD mortality.

A retrospective analysis of over 4 million admissions in the VA system demonstrated that a reduction in the length of stay among patients admitted for COPD was not associated with a higher 30-day readmission rate, suggesting that earlier discharge is not associated with at least this marker of quality of care.
An elevated d-dimer in patients with COPD exacerbation but no evidence of VTE was a bad prognostic indicator. Median survival was 9.6 months if above 1.52 mg/L and 62.6 months if below 1.52 mg/L.

Based on 2018 data from the International Thoracic Organ Transplant Registry, the median survival for lung transplantation in all COPD patients has increased to 5.9 years. Survival is longer for patients receiving a bilateral lung transplant than a single lung transplant (50% survival to 7 years vs. 5 years, respectively).
Prognosis following lung transplantation, with respect to cell rejection and survival, appears similar for patients with and without alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.

Although routine monitoring of patients with COPD has not shown long-term benefits, GOLD 2024 guidelines recommend outcome assessment to include discussion of patient goals and expectations, assessment of symptoms (consider use of a questionnaire) and frequency and severity of exacerbations, yearly spirometry, assessment of functional/exercise capacity (eg, 6-minute walking distance), addressing smoking cessation as indicated, and discussing the current therapeutic regimen including effectiveness, inhaler technique, side effects and adherence. Additional considerations include reviewing self-management and action plan, assessing need for oxygen therapy, managing co-morbidities, and providing or referring for appropriate vaccinations.
For patients on long-term oxygen therapy, GOLD 2021 recommends rechecking in 60-90 days to determine if supplemental oxygen is still needed and effective.
Exercise tolerance can be assessed by cycle ergometry or treadmill or self-paced, timed walking tests discussed above.

To monitor progress with respect to quality of life, evidence supports use of the following disease specific instruments: Chronic Respiratory Questionnaire (CRQ), COPD Assessment Test (CAT), Saint George Respiratory Questionnaire (SGRQ), and Living with COPD questionnaire (LCOPD).
A shorter 10-item questionnaire, the Clinical COPD Questionnaire, can also be used to measure health-related quality of life and compared favorably with the first three instruments noted above.

Patient-reported measures of functional status appear better than performance-based measures. The former may be best measured by the functional performance inventory (FPI), functional performance inventory short form (FPI-SF), living with COPD questionnaire (LCOPD), COPD activity rating scale (CARS), University of Cincinnati dyspnea questionnaire (UCDQ), shortness of breath with daily activities (SOBDA), or the short-form pulmonary functional status scale (PFSS-11). The best-rated performance-based measures are the 6-minute walk test (6MWT), endurance treadmill test, and usual 4-meter gait speed (usual 4MGS).

De-escalation of ICS is suggested by GOLD 2024 for patients who are doing well at follow-up, although they caution that for those with elevated eosinophil counts, discontinuation is more likely to be associated with development of exacerbations. ATS recommends withdrawal of ICS after 1 year in patients who do well.

In an RCT of 2485 patients with a history of COPD exacerbation given 6 weeks of tiotropium, salmeterol and ICS, withdrawal of the ICS did not result in a difference with respect to the first moderate or severe COPD exacerbation.

In an ad hoc analysis of the IMAPCT trail comparing duel to triple therapy, among 7,360 patients who were prior ICS users, excluding the first 30 days of randomization to reduce early effects of ICS withdrawal, patients who continued on triple therapy vs. LAMA/LABA had fewer moderate-severe exacerbations at 1 year (19% reduction; 0.98 vs. 1.38, respectively). In addition, among both prior ICS users and nonusers, patients in the triple therapy treatment arm experienced the greatest reduction in Saint George Respiratory Questionnaire scores, a measure of quality of life, at all timepoints.

algorithm.title: Approach to the Patient with Suspected COPD.

cell.label: Patient who smokes and has chronic cough or symptoms suspicious for COPD (persistent, progressive, or exertional dyspnea or chronic sputum production) Less than age 45 years or strong family history of COPD?

Assess reversible risk factors, counsel to quit smoking, avoid home and occupational hazards, and use protective equipment Provide vaccination for influenza, COVID-19, pneumococcal (if never received), and shingles. Obtain spirometry FEV1 ≥80% predicted with 0-1 moderate exacerbations and few symptoms?
Stage 1 ( Gold A): Provide patient education; exercise prescription; as needed short- or long-acting inhaled bronchodilator. Improving?
Gold B: Prescribe dual long-acting inhaled bronchodilator therapy (long-acting beta-agonist [LABA] and/or anticholinergic [LAMA]); pulmonary rehabilitation. Improving?
GOLD E: Begin with combination LABA/LAMA, pulmonary rehabilitation. Assess oxygen need. Consider referral.

Consider alternate diagnosis and additional testing (CXR, chest CT, echocardiogram). If COPD confirmed, add inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) for patients with repeated exacerbations (triple therapy), particularly for those with high blood eosinophil counts (>300 cells/microL), or if lower eosinophil count (<100 cells/mL), add azithromycin if former smokers or roflumilast in patients with chronic bronchitis and an FEV1 <50% of predicted.
